Make Claude Code remember between sessions

A new Claude Code session starts with no memory of the last one. Three ways to give it persistent memory across sessions - CLAUDE.md, the built-in auto memory, and a shared memory every session is briefed from - and where each one stops.

Steps for

On this page
  • What Claude Code remembers by itself
  • Where each one is stored
  • Where the built-in memory stops
  • What a shared memory adds
  • Set it up
  • Check that it remembers
  • Which one to use

A new Claude Code session starts with an empty context window. It knows nothing of the last one unless something loads it again. There are three ways to do that: a CLAUDE.md you write, the auto memory Claude Code keeps for itself, and a shared memory, such as Seamless, that every session, subagent, and client is briefed from. This page says what each one carries into the next session, where it stops, and how to set up the third.

(claude --continue reopens the last conversation itself. This page is about what a fresh session knows.)

The first two are built in and free, and worth using whatever else you add. What this page says about them was checked against Anthropic's memory documentation in November 2026.

What Claude Code remembers by itself

CLAUDE.md is a file of instructions you write. Claude Code reads it at the start of every session, and re-reads the project-root file from disk after a compaction, so it is the right home for standing rules: build commands, conventions, the shape of the codebase. It is yours to maintain. Anthropic suggests keeping each file under 200 lines, because a longer one uses more context and is followed less closely.

Auto memory is notes Claude Code writes for itself, from your corrections and preferences. It is on by default in local sessions and stored as plain markdown under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/: a MEMORY.md index and one topic file per memory. The first 200 lines or 25KB of the index load at session start, and Claude opens a topic file when it needs one. You can read and edit all of it with /memory.

If you work in one repository, on one computer, with Claude Code alone, those two may be all you need.

Where each one is stored

Where it lives Who writes it Loaded
CLAUDE.md In the repository, or ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for every project You Every session, in full
Auto memory ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/ Claude The first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md, at session start
Seamless ~/.seamless/memory/<project>/, one file per memory Your agents A briefing within a token budget at session start, then what matches each prompt

Where the built-in memory stops

Each of these is from Anthropic's page, not a guess:

  • One computer. Auto memory is machine-local. It is not shared across machines or cloud environments.
  • One repository. Every repository has its own memory directory, so a rule learned in one project is unknown in the next.
  • Not subagents. The main conversation's auto memory is not loaded into subagents. A fork is the exception, and a subagent can be given a memory of its own, which is a separate directory.
  • A limit on the index. Only the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md load. Anything past the limit is dropped at the next load, so Claude Code asks Claude to shorten the file as it gets close.
  • Its own judgment. Claude decides what is worth saving and does not save something every session, so whether a lesson was kept is something you find out later.
  • One client. It is Claude Code's own store. Codex keeps a separate one and reads neither.

None of this is a defect. It is a memory for one client in one place, and it does that job.

What a shared memory adds

Seamless keeps the same kind of knowledge in one store that every agent you run reads and writes:

  • Every client is briefed from it. A hook injects a <seam-briefing> into each new Claude Code and Codex session before the first prompt. What a Claude Code session saved on Monday is in a Codex session's briefing on Tuesday. See Share memory between Claude Code and Codex.
  • Rules cannot fall out. A memory of kind constraint is never dropped from its project's briefing to fit the token budget that trims everything else. The first four print in full and the rest are listed by name. See Sessions & briefings.
  • Subagents are briefed too. Every Task subagent starts with the pinned constraints and the memories that match its task.
  • Each prompt pulls what fits. Your prompt is matched against the store, and a memory that fits arrives with it as a <seam-recall> block.
  • A compaction does not lose it. The session-start hook also fires after a compaction, so the briefing lands again.
  • The work is remembered, not only the knowledge. Plans, their steps, and what the last session left open are in the briefing, so continue where we left off has something to continue from. See Tasks & plans.
  • More than one computer, when you want it. By default everything stays on one computer. In a networked install one computer keeps the data and the others connect to it, so a laptop and a desktop share one memory.
  • The handoff is written for you. What a session learned is harvested when it ends and listed under Recent findings in the next briefing, so the next session sees where the last one stopped without a HANDOFF.md you keep by hand.
  • Forgetting is yours to approve. A memory is replaced by a newer one and stays readable, and the gardener only proposes merges and retirements.

It runs beside CLAUDE.md and auto memory rather than instead of them. Keep your standing instructions in CLAUDE.md; Seamless holds what gets learned and decided along the way.

One thing no memory changes: a rule that is loaded can still be ignored. Anthropic says of CLAUDE.md that Claude "reads it and tries to follow it, but there's no guarantee of strict compliance", and the same goes for a briefing. What Seamless adds is that the rule, or at least its name, is in front of every session and subagent, and again after a compaction. For a step that must never be skipped, write a hook, which runs whatever the model decides.

Set it up

macOSLinux

curl -fsSL https://thereisnospoon.org/install | sh

Windows

irm https://thereisnospoon.org/install.ps1 | iex

The installer wires the clients it finds. Restart Claude Code once and open it in a repository:

cd ~/code/myrepo && claude

The session opens with a <seam-briefing> block. The Quickstart shows what it looks like and what to check if it is missing.

Check that it remembers

Tell the session one rule:

Save this to Seamless as a constraint: migrations run before the deploy, never after.

Then end the session, start a fresh one in the same repository, and read the top of its briefing. The rule is there, before you have typed anything, and it is also a file you can open:

ls ~/.seamless/memory/

From here the agent writes on its own when it learns something worth keeping. First prompts to try has more requests to paste, including one that reads your past Claude Code sessions for the decisions worth keeping.

Which one to use

If you want Use
Standing instructions you wrote, loaded every session CLAUDE.md
Claude Code to note your preferences without setup Auto memory
The same knowledge in Claude Code, Codex, and subagents Seamless
Rules that are in front of the agent every session Seamless constraints, or a short CLAUDE.md
Plans and open work carried into the next session Seamless
Parallel agents that do not pick the same task Seamless: see Coordinate multiple agents

For the same comparison across other memory tools, see Seamless and the alternatives.
